title: Stop Being So Positive!
subtitle: The paradox of positive thinking for people who feel terrible
body_html:
“Just perk up!”—can you imagine if this was advice that worked? And it should, if people who are feeling terrible, could look up, see the bright and sunny day, and feel better, things would be a lot easier. They are not.

There is a built-in paradox in trying to get people who feel bad to feel better. The thing most people will do is to tell people that “it's going to get better.” The irony? This is both true and absolutely the wrong thing to say. One of the reasons ‘60s counterculture adherents were so cloying was their relentless positivity.

“If you want to change the way people respond to you, change the way you respond to people.”
― Timothy Leary

The problem with telling anyone “it's going to be all right” is mistrust. We are all running a program in our brain, essentially, that combines everything we're hearing with an X factor—should this New Information be Trusted?

We base our trust of any given piece of information not on what's contained in that information itself, but overwhelmingly on our trust in the individual conveying it.

Peter Fonagy, Ph.D., the CEO of the Anna Freud Centre, refers to this as “epistemic trust.” In other words, trust in social information. on average, it's dangerous to trust other people. If you just simply trusted everybody who came up to you on the street, all your money would be gone in an afternoon. Mistrust is adaptive. Scammers don't try to build trust for no reason. They try to build trust because that's the currency to get you to do any other thing they want you to do. this is why pig-buttering scams work so well; they spend months building trust and building a relationship because it becomes harder and harder for us to imagine the person who spent endless time getting to know us means to do us harm.

If scammers can figure this out, you'd think those of us of Goodwill could figure it out too, but it seems we have more difficulty.

“Look on the bright side!”

HELL NO. We respond quietly in our heads.

The trick scammers use is able to be repurposed to virtuous. If we start any conversation by trying to understand where the other person is coming from, we build trust.

To understand the role of trust, imagine the following conversation between some fictional characters:

Darth Vader (speaking to Lando Calrissian): “I am altering the deal. Pray I don’t alter it further.”

Me ( piping in): “It seems like getting his way is really important here?”

Lando: “look, I got you, your money is coming any day now.”

Me: “it seems like Lando had some expectations here, which can be kind of hard. Lando, I'm going to ask you to hold on for a minute. Lord Vader, if I'm hearing you correctly, it seems like the deal matters less to you than the outcome?”

DV: “We will have what we want. No one stands in our way.”

Me: “The last people who stood in your way got vaporized into nothingness on Alderaan!”

Lando: “The money is on its way! Trust me.”

DV: “Well, the man said to trust him, and that's what I'm gonna do. Thanks for letting me know that everything is going to be OK eventually, I'm just gonna head back to the death star and let the Emperor know that the check is in the mail.”

That kind of blind trust would not be adaptive for the Lord Vader. Mistrust was kind of his jam. The key is to know when trust, and when not to trust. We need to have a bullsh*t meter. But it also can't stay broken in the position of permanent mistrust, or be endlessly trusting.

Our brains have solved this problem by learning to trust people, and thus the words that come out of their mouth, not relying on the message alone. This is a good example of why the uptake on AI that hallucinates—or, in human terms, lies to you—misses a key motivation for humans.

We want the truth. Sometimes we can't handle the truth, but we want it anyway.

Thus, for people who have an experience of chronic depression, or unhelpful mental health treatment, it's adaptive to hold mistrust for messages of hope. For other individuals, for whom life has been more kind, hearing a positive affirmation or hope for the future might be a completely different experience in the opposite direction.

There is a solution to not knowing how hopeful you can afford to be with somebody! It's to be unsure, and to take acknowledging someone's experience as a starting place.

“How are you feeling?”

“Pretty bad, honestly”

“it sounds like you're feeling pretty bad!”

“yeah, thanks for hearing me out.”

“are you worried that it's gonna get better?”

“pretty sure that's the case!”

[It's at this point that we take a different tactic than telling this individual it's going to get better!]

“that sounds pretty dark. What's it like to be in such a dark place?”

The secret to being the most supportive when you don't know how much hope someone wants to hear? Reflect back what you heard, and be curious about their experience. That's it. Nothing fancy.
